library(dplyr)

title: What Should a Budget-Conscious Reader Browse First?
text:
The question
Online stores offer thousands of choices, but a low sticker price is not necessarily a good value. A reader with a £20 ceiling probably wants both affordability and some evidence of quality. I therefore asked: Which book categories give a budget-conscious shopper the best chance of finding a highly rated book for £20 or less?
The data come from Books to Scrape, a fictional bookstore created specifically for web-scraping practice. Because the site is a sandbox rather than a real retailer, the exercise is ethical and reproducible; no login, CAPTCHA, or access restriction is bypassed. The prices and ratings are fictional, so the recommendation demonstrates a decision method rather than advice about today’s real book market.

title: What Should a Budget-Conscious Reader Browse First?
text:
Collecting and cleaning the catalog
I used rvest to read the home page and extract links to every category. The scraper then visited each category page, followed its “next” link, and paused 0.35 seconds between requests. From every product card it collected the full title, price, star-rating class, stock status, and URL. The complete scraping code is in scrape_analyze.R; its core extraction step is shown below.
page <- read_html(url)
cards <- html_elements(page, "article.product_pod")

tibble(
  title = html_attr(html_element(cards, "h3 a"), "title"),
  price_gbp = parse_number(html_text2(html_element(cards, ".price_color"))),
  rating_word = str_remove(
    html_attr(html_element(cards, "p.star-rating"), "class"),
    "star-rating\\s+"
  )
)
The rating words (“One” through “Five”) were converted to integers, pound signs were removed from prices, and duplicate product URLs were dropped. Validation checks require exactly 1,000 books and no missing prices or ratings. I defined a budget-quality book as one rated four or five stars and priced at no more than £20. To avoid a misleading win by a tiny niche, category comparisons include only categories containing at least 10 books.

title: What Should a Budget-Conscious Reader Browse First?
text:
Results
Across the catalog, 1000 books appeared in 50 categories. 7.5% of all books met both the quality and price thresholds. The figure ranks the ten strongest eligible categories by the share of their inventory that met both conditions.



Budget-quality availability by category.


category_summary |>
  slice_head(n = 5) |>
  transmute(
    Category = category,
    Books = books,
    `Median price` = dollar(median_price_gbp, prefix = "£"),
    `Average rating` = round(average_rating, 2),
    `Budget-quality share` = percent(budget_quality_share, accuracy = 1)
  ) |>
  kable(align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"))

Poetry ranks first: 21% of its listings clear both hurdles, compared with 8% catalog-wide. Its median price is £38.77. A shopper who is flexible about genre should start there, then compare the next few categories in the table. Someone choosing a specific title can use the generated recommendations.csv, which sorts in-stock qualifying books by rating and then price.
This ranking is descriptive, not a claim that price causes ratings or that star ratings measure literary merit. Books to Scrape also provides no review counts, so a five-star item cannot be weighted by the amount of feedback behind it. Different cutoffs would change the ranking; £20 and four stars simply make the shopping rule explicit and easy to revise in the script.

title: What Should a Budget-Conscious Reader Browse First?
text:
Takeaway
Web scraping becomes useful when it is tied to a decision rule. Here, rvest transformed paginated product cards into a clean catalog, while a combined price-and-quality threshold turned that catalog into a browsing recommendation. For a £20 shopper in this simulated store, begin with Poetry, where the probability of finding an affordable, highly rated option is greatest among categories with a meaningful selection. The same workflow could be reused on a permitted real catalog—after checking its terms and robots.txt—to guide an actual purchase.

title: What Should a Budget-Conscious Reader Browse First?
text:
Related research
This project is a small-scale example of a broader use of web-scraped prices in economic research. Cavallo and Rigobon’s Billion Prices Project collected online prices to construct daily inflation indexes across multiple countries. Their research shows that web data can supplement traditional price statistics by providing information more frequently. In another study, Aparicio and Cavallo used scraped supermarket prices to examine how price controls affected inflation, product availability, and price dispersion in Argentina. The present analysis asks a simpler consumer-level question, but it follows the same general process: collect online product information, create a transparent comparison measure, and translate the results into a practical decision.

title: Why Do Students Who Study More Appear to Have Lower GPAs?
text:
Students are usually told that studying more leads to better grades. Yet a simple regression can tell the opposite story. In my simulated dataset of 3,000 students, one additional hour of weekly study is associated with a 0.018-point decrease in college GPA. Should students close their textbooks?
Not so fast. This surprising result illustrates omitted variable bias: a regression coefficient can absorb the influence of an important variable that was left out of the model.

title: Why Do Students Who Study More Appear to Have Lower GPAs?
text:
How the Data Were Simulated
I generated 3,000 fictional students using a fixed random seed. Each student was assigned a high school GPA, attendance rate, sleep duration, stress level, weekly study time, and college GPA. Study time was designed to be higher among students with weaker prior preparation or lower attendance. College GPA was designed to increase with both prior preparation and study time: before applying the 0–4 GPA boundary, one additional weekly study hour contributed 0.075 points. Random noise ensured that students with similar backgrounds did not receive identical outcomes.
This design deliberately creates confounding for illustration. It shows how omitted variable bias can arise, but it does not estimate the real-world effect of studying.

title: Why Do Students Who Study More Appear to Have Lower GPAs?
text:
A Misleading First Impression
I simulated students’ weekly study hours and college GPAs, together with four background characteristics: high school GPA, attendance, sleep, and stress. The simulation deliberately represents a plausible pattern: students with weaker academic preparation tend to study longer because they need more time to master the same material. At the same time, prior preparation directly predicts college GPA.
The complete analysis is available in the reproducible R script, and the simulated dataset contains no real student records.


Show code
naive_model <- lm(college_gpa ~ study_hours, data = students)

adjusted_model <- lm(
  college_gpa ~ study_hours + high_school_gpa + attendance +
    sleep_hours + I((sleep_hours - 7)^2) + stress + I(stress^2),
  data = students
)





The naive relationship is negative, but the estimated effect becomes positive after student background is taken into account.


The red line in the upper panel slopes downward. However, the colors reveal what that line hides: students with lower high school GPAs are concentrated toward the right because they generally study longer, while students with stronger preparation can earn high college GPAs with fewer hours.

title: Why Do Students Who Study More Appear to Have Lower GPAs?
text:
Where the Bias Comes From
Let \(Y\) be college GPA, \(D\) be study hours, and \(A\) be prior academic preparation. The relationship of interest is
\[Y = \beta D + \gamma A + \varepsilon.\]
If preparation is excluded, its influence does not disappear. Instead, some of it enters the estimated coefficient on study hours. Here, preparation raises college GPA but is negatively related to study time. The naive regression therefore mixes the positive effect of studying with the negative association between studying and prior preparation.
Once I control for observed student characteristics, the estimated effect changes from −0.018 to +0.071 GPA points per additional weekly study hour. The comparison is now between students with similar backgrounds rather than between fundamentally different students.

title: Why Do Students Who Study More Appear to Have Lower GPAs?
text:
Where Double Machine Learning Enters
An ordinary regression requires the analyst to specify how every control variable enters the model. That becomes difficult when there are many controls or nonlinear relationships. Double machine learning (DML) uses flexible prediction models to remove the part of both GPA and study time that can be explained by the observed background variables.
First, a machine-learning model predicts GPA from the controls. A second model predicts study hours from the same controls. DML then relates the two sets of unexplained residuals. I used XGBoost with five-fold cross-fitting, so each student’s residual was produced by a model that was trained on other students. This reduces the risk that overfitting contaminates the final estimate.
The DML estimate is +0.070, with a 95% confidence interval from +0.065 to +0.076. It is close to both the adjusted regression estimate and the true effect of +0.075 used to generate the data.

title: Why Do Students Who Study More Appear to Have Lower GPAs?
text:
What DML Cannot Do
DML is not a machine that automatically discovers causality. It can flexibly adjust for variables that were measured, but it cannot recover information that was never recorded. If motivation or family support affects both study time and GPA but is absent from the data, the estimate may still be biased.
The larger lesson is simple: a regression coefficient does not interpret itself. Before concluding that studying lowers GPA—or that any behavior causes an outcome—we should ask who is being compared and which relevant differences have been left out.

title: How Has Labor-Force Participation Changed Across Age Groups?
text: The U.S. labor-force participation rate measures the share of the civilian population that is either employed or actively looking for work. Unlike the unemployment rate, it also captures decisions to enter or leave the labor market. This post asks how participation changed from 2000 to 2024 and whether those changes differed across age and gender groups. The results reveal three connected trends: participation fell substantially among young people, rose among older adults, and became more similar for prime-age men and women.

title: How Has Labor-Force Participation Changed Across Age Groups?
text: The U.S. labor-force participation rate measures the share of the civilian population that is either employed or actively looking for work. Unlike the unemployment rate, it also captures decisions to enter or leave the labor market. This post asks how participation changed from 2000 to 2024 and whether those changes differed across age and gender groups. The results reveal three connected trends: participation fell substantially among young people, rose among older adults, and became more similar for prime-age men and women.

title: How Has Labor-Force Participation Changed Across Age Groups?
How Has Labor-Force Participation Changed Across Age Groups?
section: Participation moved in opposite directions across ages
text:
Participation moved in opposite directions across ages



Annual labor-force participation rates for four age groups from 2000 through 2024.


The age-group trends are strikingly different. Participation among people ages 16–24 fell from 66.0% in 2000 to 56.3% in 2024, a decline of 9.8 percentage points. The series reached its lowest point, 53.7%, in 2020. In contrast, participation among people ages 55–64 increased from 59.6% to 66.3%. Participation among adults age 65 and older also rose, from 13.2% to 19.9%, although it peaked at 20.7% in 2019. Prime-age participation was comparatively stable: the rate for ages 25–54 was 84.0% in 2000 and 83.7% in 2024.

title: How Has Labor-Force Participation Changed Across Age Groups?
text:
The prime-age gender gap narrowed



Prime-age labor-force participation rates for men and women from 2000 through 2024.


Among adults ages 25–54, men continued to participate at a higher rate than women, but the difference became smaller. The gap declined from 15.0 percentage points in 2000 to 11.1 points in 2024. Male participation fell from 91.7% to 89.3%, while female participation rose from 76.7% to 78.1%. Both series dropped during economic downturns, including 2020, but the longer-run convergence is clear.

title: How Has Labor-Force Participation Changed Across Age Groups?
section: The life-cycle curve shifted most at the edges
text:
The life-cycle curve shifted most at the edges



Labor-force participation over the life cycle in 2000, 2019, 2020, and 2024.


The age profiles show that participation remains highest from the late twenties through the early fifties. The largest changes occurred outside those prime working ages. For ages 16–19, participation fell from 52.4% in 2000 to 37.2% in 2024. For ages 65–69, it rose from 25.1% to 34.0%. These shifts are consistent with longer schooling at younger ages and longer working lives at older ages, although the descriptive CPS evidence alone cannot establish those explanations as causal.

title: How Has Labor-Force Participation Changed Across Age Groups?
text:
Takeaway
The national labor-force participation rate conceals major differences across demographic groups. Between 2000 and 2024, younger people became less likely to participate, older adults became more likely to work or seek work, and the prime-age gender gap narrowed. These patterns have important practical implications. Greater participation among older adults may help offset some labor-supply pressures created by population aging, but it also increases the importance of flexible schedules, age-friendly workplaces, retirement policy, and access to health care. Lower participation among younger people may partly reflect greater educational enrollment, but it may also raise concerns about delayed work experience and access to entry-level jobs. Meanwhile, the remaining prime-age gender gap suggests that child care, paid leave, and workplace flexibility may still influence labor-market participation. Overall, policymakers and employers should look beyond the national average and consider the distinct barriers and incentives facing different demographic groups.
Data source: IPUMS CPS. Complete reproduction code is available in the GitHub repository, including the data-processing script and figure script.

title: Does Getting Richer Buy Longer Lives?
text: Money seems to buy longer lives, but only up to a point. Across 153 countries in 2023, richer countries generally had higher life expectancy. Yet countries that experienced the fastest economic growth since 2000 did not necessarily make the largest gains in longevity. Using World Bank data, I examine how the relationship differs when countries are compared at one point in time versus followed over time.This question matters because rising income is often treated as a sign that people’s lives are improving. But if countries can become richer without seeing similar gains in life expectancy, income alone may not tell us enough about their progress.

title: Does Getting Richer Buy Longer Lives?
text: Money seems to buy longer lives, but only up to a point. Across 153 countries in 2023, richer countries generally had higher life expectancy. Yet countries that experienced the fastest economic growth since 2000 did not necessarily make the largest gains in longevity. Using World Bank data, I examine how the relationship differs when countries are compared at one point in time versus followed over time.This question matters because rising income is often treated as a sign that people’s lives are improving. But if countries can become richer without seeing similar gains in life expectancy, income alone may not tell us enough about their progress.

title: Does Getting Richer Buy Longer Lives?
text:
Data and method
I use three indicators from the World Bank World Development Indicators: life expectancy at birth, total population, and GDP per capita at purchasing-power parity. GDP is measured in constant 2021 international dollars. This adjusts for inflation and differences in price levels, making cross-country and over-time comparisons more meaningful than values measured in current U.S. dollars.
The data were downloaded through the official World Bank API with the WDI R package. I compare 2000 with 2023, the latest year with broad coverage across all three measures. World Bank regional aggregates are removed. For the scatterplots, I keep countries with at least one million residents in 2023 so that very small economies do not dominate the visual comparison. The repository preserves the raw download, metadata, validation results, cleaned data, and complete R scripts.


Code
# Download the indicators from the World Bank API
wdi_raw <- WDI(
  country = "all",
  indicator = c(
    gdp_per_capita = "NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD",
    life_expectancy = "SP.DYN.LE00.IN",
    population = "SP.POP.TOTL"
  ),
  start = 2000,
  end = 2023,
  extra = TRUE
)

panel <- wdi_raw |>
  filter(region != "Aggregates") |>
  arrange(country, year)

title: Does Getting Richer Buy Longer Lives?
section: Richer countries tend to live longer
text:
Richer countries tend to live longer



GDP per capita and life expectancy across countries in 2023. Bubble size represents population and color represents World Bank region.


The first figure shows a strong positive relationship between income and life expectancy. Across the 153 countries in the 2023 sample, the correlation between log GDP per capita and life expectancy is 0.88. However, the pattern begins to flatten at higher income levels. Moving from a low-income to a middle-income country is associated with a large difference in life expectancy, while income differences among wealthier countries are associated with much smaller gaps.
The colors also show that countries from the same region tend to cluster together. Regional differences explain part of the overall pattern, but they do not fully account for it: income and life expectancy are still positively related within most regions.
The United States stands out. Although it has one of the highest levels of GDP per capita, its life expectancy is lower than that of several less wealthy countries. This suggests that economic resources can support better health, but higher income does not automatically translate into longer lives.


Code
latest <- panel |>
  filter(year == 2023, population >= 1e6) |>
  drop_na(gdp_per_capita, life_expectancy)

ggplot(latest, aes(gdp_per_capita, life_expectancy)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = population, color = region), alpha = 0.72) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(
    x = "GDP per capita, constant 2021 international dollars",
    y = "Life expectancy at birth (years)"
  )

title: Does Getting Richer Buy Longer Lives?
text:
Progress differed across large countries



Life expectancy in 2000 and 2023 for the ten most populous countries. Labels show the change in years.


Life expectancy increased in all ten of the most populous countries between 2000 and 2023, although the size of the increase varied considerably. The median gain was 6.0 years. Bangladesh gained about 12.6 years and India gained about 9.3 years, while the United States gained only about 1.7 years. These differences show that improvements in health were far from equal across countries.

title: Does Getting Richer Buy Longer Lives?
section: Growth alone does not explain health gains
text:
Growth alone does not explain health gains



Changes in real GDP per capita and life expectancy from 2000 to 2023. The dashed line is a linear fit.


The third figure shows almost no relationship between income growth and improvements in life expectancy. Across 151 countries, the correlation is only 0.04, meaning that the countries with the fastest economic growth were not necessarily the ones with the largest gains in longevity. China, for example, experienced rapid income growth but a more moderate increase in life expectancy, while several African countries added many years of life with much smaller increases in income.
One possible explanation is that health improvements do not always require equally large increases in national income. In countries starting with lower life expectancy, wider access to vaccines, clean water, basic medical care, and maternal health services can produce substantial gains. Countries already near the top have less room to improve. Economic growth may also be concentrated among certain industries or groups, so a higher GDP does not automatically mean that most people receive better health care. The figure therefore suggests that how resources are used may matter as much as how quickly the economy grows.


Code
changes <- panel |>
  filter(year %in% c(2000, 2023)) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = year,
    values_from = c(gdp_per_capita, life_expectancy)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    gdp_growth_pct =
      (gdp_per_capita_2023 / gdp_per_capita_2000 - 1) * 100,
    life_gain = life_expectancy_2023 - life_expectancy_2000
  )

cor(changes$gdp_growth_pct, changes$life_gain, use = "complete.obs")

title: Does Getting Richer Buy Longer Lives?
text:
Takeaway
The figures tell a more complicated story than “richer countries live longer.” Income and life expectancy are closely related, especially among low- and middle-income countries, but the relationship becomes weaker at higher income levels. Looking across time, the countries with the fastest economic growth did not consistently achieve the largest gains in life expectancy. Economic growth can provide resources for better health, but improvements also depend on access to medical care, public-health programs, and how widely the benefits of growth are shared. GDP per capita is therefore a useful measure of development, but it does not tell the whole story.

title: Does Getting Richer Buy Longer Lives?
text:
Questions for future research
These figures show patterns rather than causal relationships. Two possible explanations could be examined with additional data:

Public-health investment: Countries that spend more on basic health services may be better able to turn economic growth into longer lives.
Income inequality: When the benefits of growth are concentrated among a small share of the population, improvements in national income may not lead to better health for everyone.

Future research could test these ideas using data on health spending, vaccination, clean-water access, and income inequality.

title: Does Getting Richer Buy Longer Lives?
text:
Data and reproducibility
The data come from the World Bank World Development Indicators and were downloaded through the official API using the WDI R package. The repository includes the data-download script, the analysis and figure script, the saved data, and all three figures. The results are descriptive and should not be interpreted as causal estimates.

title: Where Is America Growing?
text:
POPULATION SHIFT
Between 2020 and 2025, U.S. population growth was geographically concentrated rather than evenly distributed. This article asks where counties grew or shrank—and how closely that pattern followed domestic migration.

title: Where Is America Growing?
text:
Why geography matters
Population change affects local tax bases, labor markets, housing demand, school enrollment, and infrastructure needs. A national growth rate hides the fact that one county can be adding residents while another is losing them. Mapping the change lets us see whether growth forms regional clusters rather than isolated local exceptions.
I use the U.S. Census Bureau’s Vintage 2025 Population Estimates, which provide consistent county population estimates and components of change from 2020 through 2025. County and state geometry comes from the Census Bureau’s 2025 Cartographic Boundary Files. The script downloads both sources directly and joins them using the five-digit county GEOID.
The analysis focuses on the contiguous United States so Alaska and Hawaii do not have to be resized or repositioned in ways that obscure distance and area. Their observations remain in the original Census file but are excluded from the processed analytical sample.

title: Where Is America Growing?
text:
1. Growth formed clear regional clusters









The first map reports the percentage change in each county’s estimated population between July 2020 and July 2025:
[ = 100 ( - 1). ]
Growth is visibly clustered rather than randomly scattered. A broad arc of faster-growing counties runs through Florida, the Carolinas, Tennessee, Texas, and the Mountain West. Many declining counties appear in parts of the Great Plains, the Mississippi Delta, Appalachia, and the industrial Midwest. Metropolitan edges also often grew faster than nearby central or rural counties, although that pattern is not universal.
Across the 3109 counties and county equivalents in the sample, 60% gained population, and the median county grew by 1.1%. Those national summaries are modest, but the map shows why an average is incomplete: fast growth and decline were geographically concentrated.
Among counties with at least 20,000 residents, Kaufman County, Texas grew by 42.2%, while Yazoo County, Mississippi changed by -14%. The population cutoff is used only for these examples and the scatterplot labels; the map includes every county and county equivalent in the contiguous states.
These clusters matter economically. Sustained population gains can expand the labor force and consumer base but can also increase pressure on housing and infrastructure. Persistent losses can weaken local demand and make it harder to spread the fixed costs of schools, roads, and public services across residents. The map identifies where those pressures are likely to differ; it does not by itself explain why they occurred.

title: Where Is America Growing?
section: 2. Domestic migration followed much of the same geography
text:
2. Domestic migration followed much of the same geography
Population changes through births, deaths, international migration, and movement between U.S. counties. To isolate the last component, I average the Census Bureau’s annual net domestic migration rate from 2020-21 through 2024-25. The rate is measured per 1,000 residents, which makes counties of different sizes comparable.









The migration map resembles the growth map in important ways. Many fast-growing counties in Florida, Texas, the Carolinas, Tennessee, and the interior West also received more residents from elsewhere in the country than they lost. Conversely, several counties around large urban centers and across northern regions recorded net domestic outflows.
But the two maps are not identical. A county can lose residents to other U.S. counties and still grow through international migration or natural increase (births minus deaths). It can also attract domestic migrants without growing rapidly if deaths exceed births. Domestic migration is therefore one mechanism in the population accounting identity, not a complete explanation of county growth.

title: Where Is America Growing?
section: 3. Migration explains much of the pattern, but not all of it
text:
3. Migration explains much of the pattern, but not all of it









For counties with at least 20,000 residents, the correlation between the average annual domestic migration rate and five-year population growth is 0.84. The upward-sloping fitted line summarizes the relationship: counties with larger domestic inflows generally grew faster.
The cutoff reduces extreme percentage changes caused by very small denominators, but it does not change the mapped sample. Point size represents 2025 population, and color identifies the Census region. The regional colors reinforce what the maps show: many Southern and Western counties occupy the upper-right portion of the plot, while many Northeastern and Midwestern counties fall closer to zero growth or into the outflow half.
The remaining vertical spread is substantively important. Counties with similar domestic migration rates can have different overall growth because international migration and natural change also differ. The fitted line is descriptive and should not be interpreted as a causal effect of migration: employment growth, housing supply, amenities, taxes, climate, and population movement may influence one another.

title: Where Is America Growing?
text:
Takeaway
U.S. population change from 2020 to 2025 formed clear regional clusters. Growth concentrated across much of the South and Mountain West, while decline was common in parts of the Midwest, Great Plains, Appalachia, and Mississippi Delta. Domestic migration reinforced that redistribution without fully determining it.
For policymakers and local businesses, the implication is practical: places gaining residents may need more housing and infrastructure, while places losing residents face the difficult task of sustaining services and opportunity with fewer people.

title: Where Is America Growing?
text:
Methods, limitations, and reproducibility
All results are generated by analysis.R. The script downloads the Census CSV and KML files, retains county-level observations, calculates five-year population growth and annualized component rates, parses geographic coordinates, applies an equal-area Albers projection, joins attributes to boundaries by GEOID, and saves every figure and processed file.
Map colors are capped at -5% to 15% for population change and -15 to 30 per 1,000 for domestic migration so a few extreme counties do not flatten meaningful variation elsewhere. Capping affects only the displayed color; the processed CSV preserves exact values. Cartographic boundaries are simplified for national-scale mapping and should not be used for surveying or parcel-level work.
Population estimates are revised with each annual vintage, so later downloads may produce slightly different values. Estimates are not exact headcounts, and county-level patterns do not describe every neighborhood or household within a county. The analysis covers 2020-2025 and should not be treated as evidence about longer-run trends without examining earlier periods.

Data accessed: October 18, 2026. Sources: U.S. Census Bureau Population Estimates Program and 2025 Cartographic Boundary Files. See the README for exact replication and GitHub Pages instructions.

title: Submission checklist
text:
Before submitting, confirm the author name in index.qmd and render the webpage one final time.



Push this repository to GitHub.
Open Settings > Pages.
Under Build and deployment, select Deploy from a branch.
Select the main branch and /docs folder, then save.
Open the published URL and confirm that all four figures load.

Submit both the published blog URL and the GitHub repository URL.

title: Does Getting Richer Buy Longer Lives?
text: Money seems to buy longer lives, but only up to a point. Across 153 countries in 2023, richer countries generally had higher life expectancy. Yet countries that experienced the fastest economic growth since 2000 did not necessarily make the largest gains in longevity. Using World Bank data, I examine how the relationship differs when countries are compared at one point in time versus followed over time.This question matters because rising income is often treated as a sign that people’s lives are improving. But if countries can become richer without seeing similar gains in life expectancy, income alone may not tell us enough about their progress.

title: Does Getting Richer Buy Longer Lives?
text:
Data and method
I use three indicators from the World Bank World Development Indicators: life expectancy at birth, total population, and GDP per capita at purchasing-power parity. GDP is measured in constant 2021 international dollars. This adjusts for inflation and differences in price levels, making cross-country and over-time comparisons more meaningful than values measured in current U.S. dollars.
The data were downloaded through the official World Bank API with the WDI R package. I compare 2000 with 2023, the latest year with broad coverage across all three measures. World Bank regional aggregates are removed. For the scatterplots, I keep countries with at least one million residents in 2023 so that very small economies do not dominate the visual comparison. The repository preserves the raw download, metadata, validation results, cleaned data, and complete R scripts.


Code
# Download the indicators from the World Bank API
wdi_raw <- WDI(
  country = "all",
  indicator = c(
    gdp_per_capita = "NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD",
    life_expectancy = "SP.DYN.LE00.IN",
    population = "SP.POP.TOTL"
  ),
  start = 2000,
  end = 2023,
  extra = TRUE
)

panel <- wdi_raw |>
  filter(region != "Aggregates") |>
  arrange(country, year)

title: Does Getting Richer Buy Longer Lives?
section: Richer countries tend to live longer
text:
Richer countries tend to live longer



GDP per capita and life expectancy across countries in 2023. Bubble size represents population and color represents World Bank region.


The first figure shows a strong positive relationship between income and life expectancy. Across the 153 countries in the 2023 sample, the correlation between log GDP per capita and life expectancy is 0.88. However, the pattern begins to flatten at higher income levels. Moving from a low-income to a middle-income country is associated with a large difference in life expectancy, while income differences among wealthier countries are associated with much smaller gaps.
The colors also show that countries from the same region tend to cluster together. Regional differences explain part of the overall pattern, but they do not fully account for it: income and life expectancy are still positively related within most regions.
The United States stands out. Although it has one of the highest levels of GDP per capita, its life expectancy is lower than that of several less wealthy countries. This suggests that economic resources can support better health, but higher income does not automatically translate into longer lives.


Code
latest <- panel |>
  filter(year == 2023, population >= 1e6) |>
  drop_na(gdp_per_capita, life_expectancy)

ggplot(latest, aes(gdp_per_capita, life_expectancy)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = population, color = region), alpha = 0.72) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(
    x = "GDP per capita, constant 2021 international dollars",
    y = "Life expectancy at birth (years)"
  )

title: Does Getting Richer Buy Longer Lives?
text:
Progress differed across large countries



Life expectancy in 2000 and 2023 for the ten most populous countries. Labels show the change in years.


Life expectancy increased in all ten of the most populous countries between 2000 and 2023, although the size of the increase varied considerably. The median gain was 6.0 years. Bangladesh gained about 12.6 years and India gained about 9.3 years, while the United States gained only about 1.7 years. These differences show that improvements in health were far from equal across countries.

title: Does Getting Richer Buy Longer Lives?
section: Growth alone does not explain health gains
text:
Growth alone does not explain health gains



Changes in real GDP per capita and life expectancy from 2000 to 2023. The dashed line is a linear fit.


The third figure shows almost no relationship between income growth and improvements in life expectancy. Across 151 countries, the correlation is only 0.04, meaning that the countries with the fastest economic growth were not necessarily the ones with the largest gains in longevity. China, for example, experienced rapid income growth but a more moderate increase in life expectancy, while several African countries added many years of life with much smaller increases in income.
One possible explanation is that health improvements do not always require equally large increases in national income. In countries starting with lower life expectancy, wider access to vaccines, clean water, basic medical care, and maternal health services can produce substantial gains. Countries already near the top have less room to improve. Economic growth may also be concentrated among certain industries or groups, so a higher GDP does not automatically mean that most people receive better health care. The figure therefore suggests that how resources are used may matter as much as how quickly the economy grows.


Code
changes <- panel |>
  filter(year %in% c(2000, 2023)) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = year,
    values_from = c(gdp_per_capita, life_expectancy)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    gdp_growth_pct =
      (gdp_per_capita_2023 / gdp_per_capita_2000 - 1) * 100,
    life_gain = life_expectancy_2023 - life_expectancy_2000
  )

cor(changes$gdp_growth_pct, changes$life_gain, use = "complete.obs")

title: Does Getting Richer Buy Longer Lives?
text:
Questions for future research
These figures show patterns rather than causal relationships. Two possible explanations could be examined with additional data:

Public-health investment: Countries that spend more on basic health services may be better able to turn economic growth into longer lives.
Income inequality: When the benefits of growth are concentrated among a small share of the population, improvements in national income may not lead to better health for everyone.

Future research could test these ideas using data on health spending, vaccination, clean-water access, and income inequality.

title: Does Getting Richer Buy Longer Lives?
text:
Takeaway
The figures tell a more complicated story than “richer countries live longer.” Income and life expectancy are closely related, especially among low- and middle-income countries, but the relationship becomes weaker at higher income levels. Looking across time, the countries with the fastest economic growth did not consistently achieve the largest gains in life expectancy. Economic growth can provide resources for better health, but improvements also depend on access to medical care, public-health programs, and how widely the benefits of growth are shared. GDP per capita is therefore a useful measure of development, but it does not tell the whole story.

title: Does Getting Richer Buy Longer Lives?
text:
Data and reproducibility
The data come from the World Bank World Development Indicators and were downloaded through the official API using the WDI R package. The repository includes the data-download script, the analysis and figure script, the saved data, and all three figures. The results are descriptive and should not be interpreted as causal estimates.

title: Where Is America Growing?
section: Growth concentrated in the South and Mountain West
text:
Growth concentrated in the South and Mountain West











The map shows a broad arc of faster-growing counties through Florida, the Carolinas, Tennessee, Texas, and the Mountain West. Declines were more common in parts of the Great Plains, the Mississippi Delta, Appalachia, and the industrial Midwest. Among counties with at least 20,000 residents, Kaufman County, Texas grew by 42.2%, while Yazoo County, Mississippi changed by -14%.
A national average misses this divide. Population gains can widen a local labor force and consumer base, but also intensify pressure on housing, schools, and infrastructure. Persistent decline creates the opposite challenge: maintaining services with a smaller tax base and population.

title: Where Is America Growing?
section: Domestic migration reinforced the same geography
text:
Domestic migration reinforced the same geography











Many counties that grew quickly also received more residents from elsewhere in the United States than they lost. The strongest shared pattern appears across Florida, Texas, the Carolinas, Tennessee, and the interior West. Several counties around large urban centers and in northern regions instead recorded domestic outflows.
Migration is not the full explanation. A county can lose domestic residents yet grow through international migration or natural increase; it can also receive domestic migrants but grow slowly when deaths exceed births. Domestic migration is one important component of population change, not a causal explanation by itself.

title: Where Is America Growing?
section: Migration mattered—but did not determine every outcome
text:
Migration mattered—but did not determine every outcome











For counties with at least 20,000 residents, the correlation between average annual domestic migration and five-year population growth is 0.84. Counties receiving more domestic migrants generally grew faster, and many Southern and Western counties sit in the upper-right part of the figure.
The remaining spread matters. Counties with similar migration rates can have different growth outcomes because international migration and natural change also vary. The fitted line is descriptive—not causal. Housing supply, jobs, amenities, taxes, climate, and migration can all influence one another.

title: Where Is America Growing?
text:
Methods and limitations
I use the U.S. Census Bureau’s Vintage 2025 Population Estimates and 2025 Cartographic Boundary Files. The reproducible script downloads both sources, joins population data to counties with the five-digit GEOID, and analyzes the contiguous United States. Alaska and Hawaii are excluded from the maps so they do not need to be resized or repositioned.
Population growth is the percentage change between July 2020 and July 2025. Domestic migration is the average annual net domestic migration rate from 2020-21 through 2024-25, reported per 1,000 residents so counties of different sizes are comparable. Map colors are capped at -5% to 15% for growth and -15 to 30 per 1,000 for migration; capping affects only the display, not the underlying data.
These are Census estimates, not exact headcounts, and they are revised by later vintages. County averages can hide substantial differences within counties. The article describes patterns over 2020-2025; it does not establish that migration causes population growth.

Data accessed: October 18, 2026. Sources: U.S. Census Bureau Population Estimates Program and 2025 Cartographic Boundary Files. See the README for exact replication instructions.

title: Where Is America Growing?
section: The exceptions reveal what migration alone misses
text:
The exceptions reveal what migration alone misses











The first three counties show the dominant pattern: strong domestic inflows were the largest source of population growth. Kaufman County, Texas; Pinal County, Arizona; and Horry County, South Carolina all gained residents primarily through movement from elsewhere in the United States.
Miami-Dade County, Florida and Harris County, Texas show why the migration map cannot be read alone. Both experienced domestic outflows, but international migration and natural increase more than offset those losses. St. Louis city, Missouri provides the opposite case: domestic outflow was not offset by the other components, producing an overall decline. These examples make the central point more precise—domestic migration is a powerful contributor to geographic redistribution, but total population change has multiple sources.
